summary: Introduces the v6ops project to document all uses of IPv4 addresses in IETF standards-track and experimental RFCs. It explains the method, which RFC types were covered, and summarizes results across seven area documents. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before switching to new addresses, people made a list of every rule that mentions the old ones. This explains the plan.

questions: survey of ipv4 addresses in ietf documents
what is the ipv4 address survey
why do protocols have ipv4 dependencies
how many ietf rfc have ipv4 dependencies
subtitle: Cataloging IPv4 dependencies in IETF standards to guide the transition to IPv6.

tldr.problem: The Internet was built on IPv4 addressing, and thousands of IETF specifications depend on it. Before transitioning to IPv6, engineers needed to know exactly where those dependencies existed.
tldr.mechanism: The v6ops working group systematically read approximately 25,000 pages of IETF standards and documented every place IPv4 addresses are assumed or required, organizing findings by IETF area.
tldr.outcome: The project identified 173 RFCs out of 877 surveyed with IPv4 dependencies (about 20%), showing that the transition challenge was significant but not universal. These companion documents in seven areas guided protocol updates.

today: RFC 3789 remains informational and has not been obsoleted. It serves as an introduction to a series of seven companion documents that provide the detailed survey results by IETF area. The project's work helped guide the design of transition mechanisms and the evolution of protocols like DHCP, DNS, and routing protocols to support IPv6.

sections.title: Why Survey IPv4 Dependencies
sections.content:
RFC 3789 introduces a large project: documenting all uses of IPv4 addresses in the IETF standards track and experimental RFCs. The driving force is the inevitable transition from IPv4 to IPv6. As IPv4 address space became exhausted and the Internet grew to billions of devices, IPv6 became necessary. But many protocols, designed before the transition was planned, assumed IPv4 addresses would always be available.

The survey is an exhaustive reading of approximately 25,000 pages of specification text. It attempts to understand not just where IPv4 appears, but why it appears and whether a protocol truly depends on IPv4 or could work address-independently.
sections.eli5: There are thousands of rules for how the Internet works, and most were written when there was only one kind of address. Someone needs to read all of them and mark which ones need to change for the new addresses.

sections.title: The History of Address Exhaustion
sections.content:
IPv4 was originally designed with 8-bit network and 24-bit host addresses, as documented in RFC 760. In 1983, it was updated to introduce the familiar A, B, C, D, and E class system. Over the following decades, clever engineering extended the life of IPv4: subnetting (RFC 917, 1984), classless inter-domain routing (CIDR) in the early 1990s, and network address translation (NATs). But each solution masked the underlying reality that IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses could not scale to a global network of hundreds of billions of devices.

By the early 1990s, the IETF began designing IPv6, which offers 128-bit addresses and was intended to be automatically configurable and address-independent where possible. The challenge: thousands of existing protocols would need to be redesigned or at least updated to support both IPv4 and IPv6 during the transition.
sections.eli5: The old address system works fine for millions of computers, but the Internet grew way bigger than anyone expected. Engineers patched it up several times, but eventually they had to design completely new addresses for the whole system.

sections.title: How the Survey Was Conducted
sections.content:
The investigators examined IETF standards in order of maturity: Full Standards (61 documents), Draft Standards (68 documents), Proposed Standards (597 documents), and Experimental RFCs (144 documents). They deliberately excluded Informational RFCs, Best Current Practices, and Historic standards, focusing on active standards that might still need updates. A total of 877 RFCs were examined.

The methodology took an exhaustive approach: reading the actual RFC text, not just abstracts or titles. For each RFC, the team determined whether it actually depends on IPv4 as part of its core function or merely documents an IPv4-specific protocol that could be redesigned. Some protocols—like DNS or DHCP—had clear IPv4 dependencies but also clear paths to support IPv6.
sections.eli5: They picked a big pile of rules, read every word carefully to see which ones mention old-style addresses, and sorted them by how official and widely-used each rule is.

sections.title: Key Findings Across All Areas
sections.content:
The initial survey identified 173 RFCs with IPv4 dependencies out of 877 total (19.7%). The breakdown showed that Full Standards had the highest percentage of IPv4 dependencies (30 out of 68, or 44%), which makes sense because they are mature, widely deployed protocols that were designed decades ago. Draft Standards had 23.5% with dependencies (16 out of 68), while Proposed Standards had only 16.4% (98 out of 597).

Results varied dramatically by IETF area. The Internet Area (which includes protocols like IP itself, DNS, and DHCP) had 52 positives out of 186 RFCs (28%). The Routing Area had 23 out of 46 (50%), because nearly every routing protocol was designed for IPv4. The Security Area had only 4 out of 124 (3%), while the Sub-IP Area had zero dependencies. This variation indicated that some areas of the Internet needed much more work than others for the transition.
sections.eli5: Out of about 900 rules, roughly 170 mention old addresses. The rules used the most—the oldest and most popular ones—mention old addresses almost half the time. Newer ideas and security rules rarely mention them.

sections.title: The Long-Term Challenge
sections.content:
Beyond the immediate task of cataloging dependencies, the survey raised a deeper question: how should protocols be designed so that future address transitions are not traumatic? The current Internet model relies on a few principles: the End-to-End principle (applications should not depend on the network layer), stateless autoconfiguration (devices should be able to configure themselves), and orderly renumbering (when a site changes IP address block, all its devices should adapt smoothly).

However, most current transport-layer protocols (TCP and UDP) provide no mechanism for a connection to survive if one endpoint's address changes. This works today because addresses are relatively stable, but it suggests that future protocol designs should consider address independence earlier. The document notes that DHCP and Dynamic DNS attempt to address this but represent a departure from the original End-to-End principle.
sections.eli5: Changing addresses for the whole Internet is very hard. In the future, maybe the rules should be designed so that if a computer gets a new address, it doesn't break all its conversations.
